title: Majestic Victory: The Last Rank
summary: Walk away from the rook checks, then underpromote so capturing the rook does not stalemate the king.

nodes.question: Can the king escape the rook’s checks?
nodes.explanation: White has Kb6 and c6 against Ka1 and Rd5. The pawn can advance, but the king must choose a route that eventually escapes the rook’s skewers.

nodes.question: Which promotion avoids the last stalemate trap?
nodes.explanation: White has reached Kc2 and c7 against Ka1 and Rd4. After a queen promotion, ...Rc4+ Qxc4 would stalemate; a rook leaves a2 available.

branches.title: Walk down the board, then underpromote
commentary: Begin from the complete four-piece source board and follow the selected checking route.
c7 gets one step from promotion while controlling d8.
Rd6+ checks the king across the sixth rank.
Kb5 moves away from the rook rather than stepping onto its next skewer line.
Rd5+ follows with another rank check.
Kb4 continues down the board.
Rd4+ maintains the checking pursuit.
Kb3 heads toward the lower edge of the board.
Rd3+ is the next illustrated rook check.
Kc2 finally steps away from the checking ranks. The rook cannot use a lower rank to create the same skewer.
Rd4 is the source’s last stalemate trap before promotion.
c8=R avoids the queen’s diagonal control of a2 and prepares a mating threat on a8.
Ra4 stops that immediate a-file mating threat.
Kb3 attacks Ra4 and creates the Rc1 mating threat. The exact position is won; the source’s eventual rook surrender is not assumed to be the only legal reply.
branches.explanation: Kb3 attacks Ra4 and creates the Rc1 mating threat. The exact position is won; the source’s eventual rook surrender is not assumed to be the only legal reply.

branches.title: Promote to a queen and take the rook
commentary: Compare the source’s natural queen promotion from the exact late diagram.
c8=Q gives up the forced win by allowing a checking stalemate sacrifice.
Rc4+ checks Kc2 and offers the rook along the queen’s file.
Qxc4 is actual stalemate. Qc4 controls a2, Kc2 controls b1/b2, and Ka1 is not in check.
branches.explanation: Qxc4 is actual stalemate. Qc4 controls a2, Kc2 controls b1/b2, and Ka1 is not in check.

branches.title: Test the sacrifice against a rook
commentary: This independent representative continuation tests the same checking sacrifice after rook promotion.
c8=R retains White’s exact win without adding the queen’s diagonal control of a2.
Rc4+ offers the rook with check, as in the queen comparison.
Rxc4 captures the rook. Unlike Qxc4, the rook does not control a2 diagonally.
Ka2 is legal, so there is no stalemate. The exact rook-versus-king position is winning.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Ka2 is legal, so there is no stalemate. The exact rook-versus-king position is winning.

exercises.prompt: Why is a rook better than a queen?
exercises.answer: After ...Rc4+ Qxc4 the queen covers a2 and stalemates Ka1. A rook on c4 leaves a2 available, so the capture does not end the game in a draw.

exercises.prompt: What does the king walk accomplish?
exercises.answer: It reaches c2 after the repeated rank checks, where Black cannot create the same lower-rank skewer. White still has to solve the promotion stalemate trap afterward.

startContext: The complete four-piece source root and late promotion diagram are visually reconstructed. The selected king walk and rook promotion remain source-based; the parallel ...Rc4+ Rxc4 ...Ka2 comparison is independently supplied. Every encoded position is checked exactly, and a won endpoint is distinguished from actual mate.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
